chapter_summary:
Welcome to the world of network switching! At the heart of most local area networks (LANs) lies the network switch, a device far more intelligent and efficient than its predecessor, the hub. To truly grasp networking, it's essential to understand how switches operate at Layer 2 of the OSI model, primarily using Media Access Control (MAC) addresses to direct traffic. Unlike a hub, which simply repeats incoming data out of all its other ports, a switch intelligently learns which devices are connected to which ports. When a switch receives an Ethernet frame, it inspects the source MAC address and records it in its MAC address table (also known as a CAM table), associating that MAC address with the specific port it came from. This learning process allows the switch to build a map of the network.

When the switch then receives a frame destined for a particular MAC address, it looks up that destination MAC address in its table. If it finds a match, it forwards the frame only out of the corresponding port, significantly reducing unnecessary traffic on other ports. If the destination MAC address is not yet in its table, the switch floods the frame out of all ports (except the one it came in on), much like a hub. However, once the destination device responds, the switch learns its MAC address and adds it to the table for future directed forwarding. This intelligent forwarding is what makes switches so efficient and why they are fundamental to modern LANs.

A key concept distinguishing switches from hubs is their impact on collision domains and broadcast domains. A collision domain is a segment of a network where data packets can "collide" with one another, corrupting data and requiring retransmission. In a hub-based network, all devices connected to the hub share a single collision domain. This means that if two devices try to transmit simultaneously, a collision occurs, leading to delays and reduced performance. A switch, however, creates a separate collision domain for each port. This means that two devices connected to different ports on the same switch can transmit simultaneously without collisions, dramatically improving network performance and throughput. Each switch port essentially operates in full-duplex mode, allowing simultaneous sending and receiving.

While switches segment collision domains, they typically do not segment broadcast domains by default. A broadcast domain is a logical division of a computer network where all nodes can reach each other by broadcast at the data link layer. When a device sends a broadcast message (e.g., an ARP request to find a MAC address for a known IP address), the switch will forward that broadcast out of all its ports within the same VLAN (which we'll cover in the next chapter). All devices on that switch, or interconnected switches within the same broadcast domain, will receive the broadcast. While necessary for certain network functions, excessive broadcasts can consume bandwidth and CPU cycles on network devices, a phenomenon known as a "broadcast storm." Understanding this distinction is crucial for designing efficient and scalable networks.

To illustrate the MAC address learning process, consider the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP). When a host needs to communicate with another device on the same local network, it first needs to know the destination's MAC address, even if it already knows the IP address. The host sends an ARP request, which is a broadcast message. The switch receives this broadcast, records the source MAC address of the host that sent the ARP request, and then floods the ARP request out of all other ports. The target device receives the ARP request and responds with an ARP reply, which is a unicast message containing its MAC address. The switch then learns the MAC address of the target device and forwards the reply directly to the requesting host. Both devices' MAC addresses are now in the switch's table, enabling direct communication. You can view your own device's ARP cache using the command `arp -a` on Windows or Linux, which shows the IP-to-MAC address mappings your system has learned.

Security is also a critical consideration for switches. One common security feature is port security, which helps prevent unauthorized devices from connecting to a switch port. With port security, you can configure a switch port to allow only specific MAC addresses to transmit traffic. For example, you might configure a port to accept only the MAC address of a specific workstation. If an unauthorized device attempts to connect to that port, the switch can be configured to take action, such as shutting down the port, restricting traffic, or sending an alert. This is a vital layer of defense against rogue devices or users attempting to bypass network controls. Understanding these fundamental switching concepts is your first step towards mastering network implementation.

screens.title: Understanding Switching Fundamentals
screens.subtitle: How switches learn, forward, and shape local traffic at Layer 2

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how switches operate at Layer 2, why they replaced hubs in modern LANs, and how that affects network performance and security. A switch uses hardware MAC addresses to learn where devices live and selectively forwards frames only to the appropriate port. That learning process builds a MAC address table, which lets switches avoid the constant repetition of traffic that hubs perform. You will also see how switches change collision behavior by providing a collision domain per port while still forwarding broadcast traffic across the same broadcast domain. We will walk through a concrete ARP exchange so you can observe how frames are flooded and later become directed, and we will cover the basics of port security to protect physical switch ports against unauthorized devices. Understanding these fundamentals will help you design and troubleshoot LANs more effectively. As you move through the lesson, ask yourself: why does learning MAC addresses matter for both performance and security?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Switches forward Ethernet frames by learning MAC addresses and mapping them to switch ports, improving throughput by eliminating unnecessary traffic.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the practical differences between hubs and switches, describe how switches learn and use MAC addresses for forwarding, identify the key parts of an Ethernet frame at Layer 2, and distinguish collision domains from broadcast domains. Each objective connects to a real task: explaining why a hub creates a single collision domain helps you diagnose slow LANs; describing MAC learning lets you predict forwarding behavior when hosts join the network; recognizing frame fields helps you decode traffic during troubleshooting; and distinguishing domain types guides topology and VLAN planning later. For each objective you will see short examples and a verification milestone that ties the skill to observable behaviors — like inspecting an ARP cache, watching a switch flood then learn a MAC address, or configuring a port to accept only one MAC. These are not abstract goals; they map directly to practical troubleshooting and basic switch configuration skills you will use in entry-level network roles.

screens.title: Hub vs Switch: how forwarding differs
screens.subtitle: Why switches improve LAN performance compared to hubs

narration.text: Start with a clear definition. A hub is a Layer 1 device that repeats incoming signals to all other ports. A switch is a Layer 2 device that forwards frames selectively using MAC addresses. Concretely, if two hosts send at the same time through a hub, their signals share the same collision domain and collide, forcing retransmission. With a switch, each port is its own collision domain; two separate pairs of ports can transmit simultaneously without interference. An example: two file transfers between different port pairs on a switch can run at full speed; on a hub they would experience collisions and retransmits, causing visible slowdowns. A common misconception is that switches stop all shared traffic — they do not by default stop broadcast frames, which a hub also forwards. Broadcasts still reach all ports within the same broadcast domain. Another misconception is that switches never flood traffic; switches will flood when a destination MAC is unknown. Takeaway: switches provide per-port collision isolation and selective forwarding, so they scale much better than hubs in LANs. Consider: when you encounter a slow network segment, ask whether a shared collision domain is the root cause.

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: Switch ports act as separate collision domains, letting multiple simultaneous conversations occur without collisions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Hub vs Switch
Comparison

Hub (Layer 1)

Repeats electrical signals to all ports. All connected devices share a single collision domain, so simultaneous transmissions collide.

Collision domain: single, shared
Use case: legacy networks, testing only
Comparison

Switch (Layer 2)

Forwards frames using MAC addresses. Each physical port is its own collision domain, permitting full-duplex simultaneous send and receive.

Collision domain: per port
Use case: modern LANs for improved throughput
Example scenario
Two hosts on different switch ports transfer large files simultaneously and do not collide. On a hub both transfers would suffer collisions and retransmission delays.
Key takeaway
Switching isolates collisions per port, improving concurrency and throughput.

screens.title: How a switch learns MAC addresses
screens.subtitle: Source inspection, table entry, and mapping to ports

narration.text: Definition first: MAC learning is the process where a switch records the source MAC address of incoming frames and associates that MAC with the port on which the frame arrived. Practically, when a host sends any frame, the switch inspects the source MAC and updates its MAC address table with an entry that ties the MAC to the receiving port. Example: Host A with MAC AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF sends an ARP request. The switch records that MAC on port Gi0/1. Immediately after, the switch receives an ARP reply from Host B. If Host B's MAC was unknown, the switch had flooded the request; when the reply arrives as a unicast, the switch records Host B's MAC and now can forward future frames directly. A common misconception is that MAC tables are static; they are learned dynamically and age out after inactivity. Another misconception is that the switch inspects payloads — it only needs header MAC fields. Takeaway: MAC learning builds a dynamic map enabling directed forwarding and reducing unnecessary traffic. Ask yourself: how will the switch behave when a MAC ages out and the host sends another frame?

keyIdea.title: Learning steps
keyIdea.text: Inspect source MAC, create or update MAC table entry, associate MAC with ingress port; entries age out over time.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › MAC Learning
Process

Steps the switch follows

  1. Receive frame and read the source MAC address from the Ethernet header.
  2. Create or update a MAC table entry mapping the source MAC to the ingress port.
  3. If destination MAC is known, forward out the mapped port; if unknown, flood to other ports.
  4. Aging: entries expire after a period of inactivity and are removed.
Concrete example
Host A (AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF) on Gi0/1 sends an ARP request. Switch adds AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF → Gi0/1. When Host B replies, switch adds B's MAC and future frames are forwarded directly.
Misconception: MAC tables are permanent. Reality: entries age out and must be relearned.
Key takeaway: Dynamic MAC learning builds a mapping that enables efficient unicast forwarding.

screens.title: Forwarding behavior: directed forwarding and flooding
screens.subtitle: When switches forward to a single port and when they flood

narration.text: Here is a clear claim: switches forward frames to a specific port when the destination MAC is present in the MAC table; they flood when the destination MAC is unknown. Start with an example: a freshly powered switch has an empty MAC table. Host X sends a frame to Host Y; the switch records X's source MAC on the receiving port and then, finding Y's MAC unknown, floods the frame out of all other ports. When Y replies, the switch records Y's MAC and future frames between X and Y are forwarded directly. A common misconception is that flooding is harmful by design. Flooding is necessary to discover unknown destinations; once learned, directed forwarding reduces unnecessary traffic. Another misconception is that flooding equals broadcasting; flooding targets all ports except the ingress one but is used only for unknown unicast destinations, while broadcasts intentionally address all devices. Takeaway: flooding enables discovery; learning converts discovery into efficient unicast forwarding. Consider how this behavior affects transient traffic during network startup or after MAC table timeouts. Forwarding behavior: directed forwarding and flooding means if destination mac is in the table, forward to that port; if not, flood to discover the destination.. In practical terms, when switches forward to a single port and when they flood. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Forwarding rule
keyIdea.text: If destination MAC is in the table, forward to that port; if not, flood to discover the destination.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Forwarding Behavior
Process

Directed forwarding vs flooding

Directed forwarding occurs when destination MAC is found in the MAC table. The frame is forwarded only out of that port.
Flooding happens when the destination MAC is unknown. The switch sends the frame to all ports except the ingress port to find the destination device.
Unknown unicast flooding is distinct from a broadcast, which intentionally addresses all devices.
Example walk
Switch starts empty. Host1 sends to Host2. Switch learns Host1's MAC and floods to find Host2. Host2 replies; switch learns Host2's MAC. Later unicast traffic goes directly to Host2's port.
Key takeaway: Flooding is temporary and enables learning so direct forwarding can follow.

screens.title: Ethernet frame structure
screens.subtitle: Essential fields at Layer 2 and their roles

narration.text: An Ethernet frame is the basic data unit at Layer 2. Key fields include the destination MAC, source MAC, payload, and an error-checking field. The destination and source MAC fields are what switches inspect to learn addresses and forward frames. The payload contains higher-layer data such as an ARP request or IP packet and is not needed for basic switch forwarding. The error-checking field allows devices to detect corrupted frames and discard them. A concrete example is an ARP request: the Ethernet header carries a broadcast destination MAC, the sender's MAC in the source field, and an ARP payload that asks which device owns a given IP. A common misconception is expecting switches to read or alter payloads; switches forward based on header MAC fields only. Another misconception is that MAC addresses are logical and change frequently; MACs are hardware identifiers assigned to network interfaces. The takeaway: recognizing these fields helps you understand how switches make forwarding decisions and why ARP uses broadcasts to discover MACs. Ethernet frame structure means destination and source mac fields drive layer 2 forwarding; the payload carries higher-layer data and does not affect basic switching decisions.. In practical terms, essential fields at layer 2 and their roles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Frame essentials
keyIdea.text: Destination and source MAC fields drive Layer 2 forwarding; the payload carries higher-layer data and does not affect basic switching decisions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Ethernet Frame Structure
Definition

Important fields

  • Destination MAC: guides where the frame should go.
  • Source MAC: used by switches to learn and map ports.
  • Payload: carries ARP or IP data used by higher layers.
  • Frame check sequence: validates frame integrity.
ARP example
An ARP request is sent to the broadcast MAC. The source MAC is the requester's NIC. Switches learn the source from the request and flood the broadcast so all devices can respond if they own the IP.
Misconception: switches inspect payloads. They do not need payloads to forward; header MACs are sufficient for Layer 2 switching.

screens.title: Collision domains vs Broadcast domains
screens.subtitle: How switches affect collisions and broadcasts differently

narration.text: Make this clear: collision domains are about where simultaneous transmissions can physically collide; broadcast domains are about which devices receive broadcast frames. A hub creates a single large collision domain where any simultaneous transmitters can collide. A switch creates a collision domain per port, so collisions are minimized and full-duplex operation is possible. However, by default a switch does not segment broadcast domains. When a host sends a broadcast, such as an ARP request, the switch forwards that broadcast out of all ports within the same broadcast domain. An example: in a simple flat network, all hosts connected to a single switch receive each broadcast. The misconception to avoid is thinking switches eliminate broadcasts; they do not. Another misconception is that collision domains are irrelevant today. They still matter for legacy half-duplex links and when hubs or unmanaged repeaters are present. Takeaway: switches reduce collisions but broadcasts still propagate unless you introduce logical segmentation like VLANs in the next chapter. Collision domains vs Broadcast domains means switches segment collision domains per port but, by default, do not segment broadcast domains; broadcasts reach all ports in the same domain.. In practical terms, how switches affect collisions and broadcasts differently. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Domain difference
keyIdea.text: Switches segment collision domains per port but, by default, do not segment broadcast domains; broadcasts reach all ports in the same domain.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Collision vs Broadcast Domains
Collision Domain

Per-port isolation

A switch makes each port its own collision domain, letting devices transmit without colliding with other ports. Full-duplex removes the collision problem between two devices on a switched link.

Broadcast Domain

Shared across ports

Broadcast frames are forwarded to all ports within the same broadcast domain. Switches do not, by default, block broadcasts; logical segmentation is required to limit them.

Example
An ARP request sent by one host is broadcast and reaches all hosts through the switch. But two hosts on different switch ports can exchange unicast frames simultaneously without collisions.
Key takeaway
Switches isolate collisions but not broadcasts; plan segmentation if broadcasts become excessive.

screens.title: Observing ARP and the ARP cache
screens.subtitle: Commands to view IP-to-MAC mappings and why they matter

narration.text: Start with a definition: the ARP cache stores recently learned IP-to-MAC mappings on your host. It exists so your computer can send frames to the correct MAC when you know an IP address. A concrete example: when you ping your router, your host checks the ARP cache; if there is no mapping it sends an ARP request broadcast and waits for a reply. After the reply, the ARP cache stores the router's IP and MAC so subsequent packets go directly. Here are simple commands you can run to observe this behavior: on Windows use the print command ipconfig /all to view interfaces and physical addresses, then run arp -a to list the ARP cache. On Mac O S or Linux use ifconfig or ip a and arp -a. A misconception is that the ARP cache is permanent; it is temporary and updates when hosts reply. Closing question: after you ping a new IP and see an entry appear in arp -a, how does that change the switch's forwarding behavior for subsequent frames? Observing ARP and the ARP cache means arp populates ip-to-mac mappings so hosts can build frames addressed to the correct mac; use arp -a to inspect these entries.. In practical terms, commands to view ip-to-mac mappings and why they matter. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: ARP purpose
keyIdea.text: ARP populates IP-to-MAC mappings so hosts can build frames addressed to the correct MAC; use arp -a to inspect these entries.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Observing ARP
Code examples
# Windows
ipconfig /all
arp -a
ping 192.168.1.1  # replace with your router's IP
arp -a

# macOS / Linux
ifconfig   # or: ip a
arp -a
ping 192.168.1.1  # replace with your router's IP
arp -a
Practical notes
  • The ARP cache shows IP-to-MAC mappings your host has learned recently.
  • Pinging a device typically causes an ARP request and populates the cache when a reply arrives.
  • Clearing the ARP cache forces new ARP requests and temporary flooding on the network while discovery occurs.
Misconception: ARP entries are permanent. They age and update as hosts come and go.

screens.title: Port security basics
screens.subtitle: Restricting a switch port to specific MAC addresses

narration.text: Port security limits which MAC addresses are allowed to send frames on a physical switch port. In basic form you configure a port to allow only one or a small set of MAC addresses and choose a reaction when an unauthorized MAC appears — for example restrict traffic or disable the port. A concrete scenario: you configure Gi0/3 to accept only the MAC of a known workstation. If someone plugs a different device into Gi0/3, the switch can block that device from sending, protecting sensitive links. A common misconception is that port security prevents all spoofing. While it blocks casual unauthorized connections at the physical port, an attacker who spoofs an allowed MAC could still bypass it unless additional controls are in place. Another misconception is that port security replaces network-wide authentication; it is a local control that complements higher-layer security. Takeaway: port security is a practical first line of defense to reduce the risk of rogue devices on switch ports, especially in access-layer deployments. Port security basics means configure allowed macs per port and define a mitigation action to protect against unauthorized physical connections.. In practical terms, restricting a switch port to specific mac addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Port security
keyIdea.text: Configure allowed MACs per port and define a mitigation action to protect against unauthorized physical connections.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Port Security Basics
Definition

What port security does

Restricts which MAC addresses may transmit on a specific physical port and defines the switch's response to violations.

Allow a fixed number of MACs or specific MACs on a port.
Configure an action such as restrict traffic or shut the port when a violation occurs.
Scenario
You configure Gi0/3 to accept only a known workstation MAC. A visitor plugs in a laptop; the switch blocks the laptop's traffic or shuts the port, depending on the configured action.
Misconception: Port security is a complete defense. It's one layer; MAC spoofing and other attacks still require additional protections.

screens.title: MAC address table (CAM table) in practice
screens.subtitle: How to read entries and why they matter for troubleshooting

narration.text: Define the MAC address table: a switch's CAM table maps MAC addresses to physical ports. Each learned entry lets the switch forward frames directly to the correct port without flooding. Practically, when troubleshooting, reading the MAC table tells you which port a MAC was last seen on and can reveal mis-cabling or stale entries. Example: if a user's MAC is mapped to an unexpected port, it might indicate that the device moved or that another device is spoofing that MAC. A common misconception is treating the MAC table like a permanent directory. It is dynamic and entries expire after inactivity and may be refreshed when traffic resumes. Another useful point: when a MAC ages out, the next frame triggers flooding until the switch relearns the address. Takeaway: the CAM table is a snapshot of recent forwarding knowledge; use it to trace device locations and to confirm that learning is occurring as expected. MAC address table (CAM table) in practice means use the mac address table to trace where devices were last seen, detect unexpected mac movements, and verify forwarding paths.. In practical terms, how to read entries and why they matter for troubleshooting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CAM table use
keyIdea.text: Use the MAC address table to trace where devices were last seen, detect unexpected MAC movements, and verify forwarding paths.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › MAC Address Table
Architecture

CAM table structure

Entries map a MAC to a specific switch port. They are created from source MACs seen in frames and refreshed on traffic. Entries age out when devices are idle.
Troubleshooting example
If a user's MAC appears on the wrong port, check for misplaced cables, unauthorized devices, or spoofed addresses. Clearing stale entries and generating traffic can prove the current location of a host.
Practical check
Run the switch's show mac address-table or equivalent and verify that expected MACs map to expected ports. If entries are missing, generate traffic from the device to trigger learning.
Key takeaway: CAM entries are dynamic diagnostics that reveal where the switch last saw a MAC address.

screens.title: Broadcast storms and practical implications
screens.subtitle: Why excessive broadcasts matter and when they appear

narration.text: A broadcast storm is a situation where repeated broadcast traffic consumes significant bandwidth and processing on network devices. Broadcasts are necessary for functions like ARP, but when too many broadcasts occur, they can degrade network performance and overload switch CPUs. A common cause in flat networks is a misbehaving device that sends repeated broadcasts or a bad loop without proper prevention. Example: an application that emits excessive ARP traffic or a device stuck in repeated discovery can cause many broadcasts to traverse the switch and be delivered to every host in the broadcast domain. A misconception is assuming switches always manage broadcast load; they forward broadcasts by design and will distribute them across the broadcast domain. The takeaway is to monitor broadcast levels and use logical segmentation, which you will learn about in the next chapter, to limit broadcast scope. For now, recognize that design choices at Layer 2 influence how broadcasts affect the whole LAN. Broadcast storms and practical implications means excessive broadcasts consume bandwidth and processing; recognize symptoms and plan segmentation to limit their impact.. In practical terms, why excessive broadcasts matter and when they appear. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Broadcast storms
keyIdea.text: Excessive broadcasts consume bandwidth and processing; recognize symptoms and plan segmentation to limit their impact.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Broadcast Storms
Operational

Why broadcasts matter

Broadcasts are useful for discovery but, when excessive, consume bandwidth and CPU cycles on hosts and network devices. In a flat network, every broadcast reaches all hosts in the same broadcast domain.
Symptoms and example
Symptoms include slow response, high CPU on network devices, and many entries appearing in ARP caches. For example, a misconfigured device repeatedly sending discovery broadcasts can flood a switch and all connected hosts.
Misconception: Switches eliminate broadcast problems. They forward broadcasts by design; limiting them requires logical segmentation, which is covered next.
Key takeaway
Watch broadcast levels. Excessive broadcasts affect every device in a broadcast domain and should be controlled through design choices.

screens.title: Hands-on activity: Inspecting MACs and ARP
screens.subtitle: A guided sequence to observe MAC learning and ARP behavior

narration.text: This activity turns concepts into observable actions. First, open your terminal or command prompt. Identify your network interface and its physical MAC using ipconfig /all on Windows or ifconfig or ip a on Mac O S/Linux. Note the MAC so you can recognize it later. Next, run arp -a to view your current ARP cache and record any entries. Now ping your default gateway; this triggers an ARP request if the gateway's MAC is unknown. Run arp -a again and observe any new or updated entries. On a simple switch, you should see the ARP request flooded initially and then a unicast reply populate your ARP cache. Connect a second host to the same switch and generate traffic to see the switch learn its MAC in the CAM table. A common trap is prematurely assuming no learning occurred; ensure the host has sent traffic so the switch can record its source MAC. After the activity, reflect on how the switch's MAC table and your ARP cache enabled direct forwarding. What did you observe about flooding and subsequent direct forwarding? Hands-on activity: Inspecting MACs and ARP means observe how arp populates an arp cache and how switches learn mac addresses through actual traffic.. In practical terms, a guided sequence to observe mac learning and arp behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Observe how ARP populates an ARP cache and how switches learn MAC addresses through actual traffic.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Hands-on Activity

Step-by-step

  1. Open terminal and run ipconfig /all or ifconfig / ip a to find your MAC.
  2. Run arp -a and note current IP-to-MAC mappings.
  3. Ping your default gateway to trigger ARP if needed.
  4. Run arp -a again and compare changes.
  5. Generate traffic from another host and observe switch learning via MAC table inspection.
Notes
If a new MAC does not appear in the MAC table, ensure the host transmits frames. If ARP entries do not appear, check connectivity and repeat the ping step.
Reflection: How did the switch's learning change traffic flow after the ARP exchange?

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from switching fundamentals

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential points to remember. First, a switch forwards frames based on MAC addresses and learns those addresses from frame source fields, storing them in a MAC address table. Second, switches create separate collision domains per port, which reduces collisions and enables full-duplex operation. Third, switches do not, by default, segment broadcast domains; broadcasts and ARP requests are forwarded to all ports in the same broadcast domain. Fourth, ARP populates IP-to-MAC mappings on hosts and is visible with commands like arp -a; ARP exchanges cause flooding until addresses are learned. Fifth, port security is a local control that restricts which MACs can transmit on a given port and helps reduce unauthorized physical access. Keeping these concise facts in mind will help you diagnose LAN behavior and apply basic switch controls during troubleshooting and simple network configuration.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Switches learn MACs, forward selectively, isolate collisions, forward broadcasts, and support port-level security controls.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact cards to anchor your memory

narration.text: These three quick reminders will anchor your daily troubleshooting. First, a switch learns source MAC addresses and stores them in a MAC address table so it can forward frames directly. Second, switches create separate collision domains for each port, enabling simultaneous transmissions and full-duplex links. Third, broadcasts are forwarded to all ports in the same broadcast domain by default, so excessive broadcasts can affect the entire LAN. Keep these three ideas in mind whenever you inspect MAC tables, run arp -a, or configure simple port security. They are the core truths that explain most Layer 2 behavior you will encounter in entry-level network tasks. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means learned macs = directed forwarding; per-port collision domains = improved throughput; broadcasts travel across the broadcast domain unless segmented.. In practical terms, three compact cards to anchor your memory. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
